article_title: Why You Should Not Reuse Passwords: What Happens When One Site Gets Breached
claim: Well-run sites store passwords as salted hashes, not plain text; poorly-run sites sometimes store weaker hashes or plain text outright.
source: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet
required_correction: None — matches OWASP guidance that unique per-user salting plus a slow hash (bcrypt/Argon2id/PBKDF2) is best practice, and real-world breaches (e.g., LinkedIn 2012 unsalted SHA-1) confirm poor implementations exist.

article_title: Why You Should Not Reuse Passwords: What Happens When One Site Gets Breached
claim: Attackers run automated tools that attempt the same email-password pair across hundreds of other sites at scale using botnets; this is called credential stuffing.
source: OWASP Automated Threats — Credential Stuffing (OAT-008)
required_correction: None — matches OWASP's definition of credential stuffing as automated, botnet-driven injection of breached credential pairs against many sites.

article_title: Why You Should Not Reuse Passwords: What Happens When One Site Gets Breached
claim: Haveibeenpwned.com lets you check an email address against known breach datasets for free, and shows which specific breaches it appeared in.
source: Have I Been Pwned (haveibeenpwned.com)
required_correction: None — the free email-breach lookup and per-breach listing are accurate and match the live service.

article_title: Why You Should Not Reuse Passwords: What Happens When One Site Gets Breached
claim: Several password managers and browsers (including Chrome's Password Checkup) run a breach/reuse check automatically against your saved passwords and flag reused or breached ones.
source: Google Chrome Help — How Chrome protects your passwords
required_correction: None — Chrome's Password Checkup (on by default) checks saved passwords against known breach data and separately flags reused and weak passwords, matching the article's description.

article_title: Why You Should Not Reuse Passwords: What Happens When One Site Gets Breached
claim: The article discusses breach mechanics and haveibeenpwned generally but never cites a single actual current breach statistic (e.g., number of breaches/accounts indexed by HIBP, or a named recent breach).
required_correction: Add one concrete, sourced statistic — e.g., the current count of breaches and pwned accounts shown on haveibeenpwned.com's homepage, or a named recent large breach — as the editorial reason for this article explicitly flags this gap.

article_title: Why You Should Not Reuse Passwords: What Happens When One Site Gets Breached
claim: A well-reviewed password manager with a strong master password and its own 2FA is a smaller attack surface than dozens of reused passwords sitting exposed across old breached sites.
required_correction: Framed as a comparative risk judgment, not a checkable statistic; no correction needed, but could be strengthened with a cited security-industry recommendation.

article_title: Why You Should Not Reuse Passwords: What Happens When One Site Gets Breached
claim: Deleting unused accounts outright removes them from the pool of accounts that could eventually leak and connect back to your email.
required_correction: Reasonable practical advice but not an independently checkable factual claim; no correction needed.

article_title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
claim: Bitwarden's free tier is usable and has no meaningful feature gate.
source: Bitwarden — Personal pricing page
required_correction: None — the free plan covers unlimited passwords on unlimited devices, sync across browser/desktop/mobile/web, passkeys, generator, and breach reports with no artificial cap, matching the article's claim.

article_title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
claim: Make the master password a random-feeling but memorable phrase of 4 to 5 unrelated words rather than a short complex string.
source: NIST SP 800-63B guidance / Diceware passphrase entropy analysis
required_correction: Passphrases beat short complex strings, which is correct, but 4-5 random words is on the low end specifically for a master password protecting an entire vault; security guidance (Diceware/EFF-style wordlists) commonly recommends 6 words (~78 bits) as the floor for a master password, since 4 words can fall below 64 bits of entropy. Recommend bumping the guidance to 5-6 words minimum for this specific password.

article_title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
claim: Reputable password managers use zero-knowledge encryption: the vault is encrypted/decrypted locally with the master password, so even if the company's servers were breached, an attacker would get only encrypted data, and the company itself never has access to the master password.
source: Bitwarden — Inside zero-knowledge encryption
required_correction: The core zero-knowledge claim (master password never leaves the device, provider stores only ciphertext) is accurate for reputable managers like Bitwarden and 1Password. However, independent research (e.g., an ETH Zurich analysis) found server-side attack vectors in Bitwarden, LastPass and Dashlane that could, in some scenarios, let a malicious/compromised server undermine guarantees. Soften the absolute framing slightly to note zero-knowledge reduces but does not eliminate all server-side risk.

article_title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
claim: A growing number of sites now support passkeys, and most major password managers already store and sync these alongside traditional passwords.
source: Bitwarden — Personal pricing page (passkeys listed as a free-tier feature)
required_correction: None — passkey storage/sync is confirmed as a standard feature in Bitwarden's free tier and is broadly available in other major managers (1Password, Google Password Manager, Apple Keychain).

article_title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
claim: A small number of sites, particularly some Indian banking and government portals, disable autofill or paste functionality on their login fields for security reasons.
source: Multiple reports on Indian bank netbanking portals blocking password paste (e.g., IBTimes India, Troy Hunt's "Cobra Effect" writeup)
required_correction: None — this is a well-documented, longstanding practice among several Indian bank netbanking portals (blocking copy/paste on login fields), though it is increasingly criticized by security researchers as counterproductive.

article_title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
claim: Most password managers offer a family or team plan with secure sharing features that let you share a login without revealing the plaintext password to the other person.
source: Bitwarden — Personal pricing page (Families plan)
required_correction: None — Families/Teams plans with encrypted item sharing are standard across major password managers (Bitwarden, 1Password, Dashlane).

article_title: How to Set Up a Password Manager in 15 Minutes
claim: The fifteen-minute setup fits inside that window for the overwhelming majority of people, and once done it becomes essentially a one-time cost that runs itself passively.
required_correction: Time estimate is a subjective/typical-case claim, not independently verifiable; no correction needed, though the article itself concedes this varies with password history size.

article_title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
claim: UPI has two request types: a Pay request (you send money) and a Collect request (someone else asks you to authorize sending them money, requiring your PIN to approve); most of the article's scam scenarios (fake refund, QR-code 'receive payment' trick) rely on victims approving a Collect request.
source: NPCI circular (July 29, 2025) and subsequent reporting on discontinuation of P2P UPI Collect requests
required_correction: NPCI discontinued person-to-person (P2P) UPI Collect Requests effective October 1, 2025, specifically to curb collect-request fraud; merchant collect requests are unaffected. The article (targeting an August 2026 publish date) needs updating: the general Pay-vs-Collect / 'PIN never needed to receive money' principle still holds, but scenarios framed as an individual (a fake refund sender, an OLX buyer) sending a P2P Collect request are no longer how the scam can be executed on current UPI rails — the scam vector has likely shifted to merchant-disguised or QR-triggered Collect requests, which the article should clarify.

article_title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
claim: A common OLX-style scam has a 'buyer' ask a seller to scan a QR code and enter their PIN to 'receive' payment, which actually sends money out via a Collect request.
source: NPCI circular on P2P Collect Request discontinuation, October 1, 2025
required_correction: This specific QR-triggered P2P Collect scam mechanism was disrupted by NPCI's October 2025 discontinuation of person-to-person Collect Requests. The underlying warning (scanning a QR/entering a PIN is always a payment, never a receipt) remains valid and should be kept, but the mechanism description needs a note that NPCI has since restricted this exact P2P pathway.

article_title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
claim: No bank, UPI app, or NPCI representative will ever ask for your PIN, OTP, CVV, or app password over a phone call, SMS, or chat, for any reason.
source: RBI/bank consumer-fraud advisories (widely republished, e.g., via RBI cybersecurity awareness communications and bank customer-alert pages)
required_correction: None — this is standard, consistently repeated official guidance from RBI and Indian banks: PIN/OTP/CVV are never requested by legitimate bank or NPCI staff over call, SMS, or chat.

article_title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
claim: Fake customer care numbers walk victims through installing AnyDesk or TeamViewer, giving scammers screen access or control; no genuine bank/UPI support process requires installing a remote-access app.
source: RBI warning on AnyDesk-based fraud (reported by The Week, Zeebiz, CIO.inc)
required_correction: None — RBI issued an explicit alert to banks and customers about AnyDesk (and similar apps like TeamViewer, QuickSupport) being used by fraudsters posing as bank staff to gain remote device access; the mechanism described matches reporting closely.

article_title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
claim: Report fraud on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) or call 1930 within a few hours, as speed materially affects recovery chances.
source: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal / 1930 helpline (I4C, Ministry of Home Affairs)
required_correction: None — 1930 is the correct, current 24/7 national cyber-fraud helpline (it replaced the earlier 155260 number), developed with RBI and banks, and cybercrime.gov.in is the correct portal; speed of reporting genuinely affects the 'golden hour' fund-freezing window.

article_title: How UPI Fraud Actually Happens: The Five Warning Signs
claim: A live voice call creates more social pressure and urgency than a text message, which is why voice scams feel more convincing.
required_correction: General psychological observation, not a specific checkable statistic; no correction needed.

article_title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
claim: India's instant-loan-app fraud problem got bad enough that the RBI issued specific digital lending guidance for it.
source: RBI Guidelines on Digital Lending, 2022 (and subsequent 2025 Digital Lending Directions)
required_correction: None — RBI issued the Digital Lending Guidelines on August 10, 2022 (effective for new customers from September 2, 2022, existing loans by November 30, 2022), specifically in response to predatory app-based lending; consolidated into RBI's 2025 Digital Lending Directions.

article_title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
claim: The RBI maintains a public list of registered NBFCs on its website (rbi.org.in) that can be searched by the exact lending entity's name to verify a loan app.
source: RBI website / RBI Digital Lending Apps (DLA) directory guidance
required_correction: RBI does not publish a single list titled 'RBI Approved Loan Apps.' What it maintains is (a) a searchable register of licensed NBFCs/banks, and (b) a separately operationalised Digital Lending Apps (DLA) directory listing apps used by regulated entities. The article's instruction to 'search the RBI's NBFC list' is directionally correct but should be corrected to clarify readers must search for the registered lending entity/NBFC name (as disclosed in the app), not the app's own brand name, since RBI's list is entity-based, not app-name-based.

article_title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
claim: RBI's digital lending guidelines require every regulated lender to have a named grievance redressal officer whose contact details are disclosed within the app.
source: RBI NBFC grievance redressal requirements / RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) digital lending provisions
required_correction: None — RBI requires every regulated entity (and its lending service provider) engaged in digital lending to designate a Grievance Redressal Officer/Nodal Officer with published contact details, and this is a mandatory 'Day 0' escalation step before a complaint can go to the RBI Ombudsman.

article_title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
claim: Digital lending guidelines require regulated lenders to offer a cooling-off or look-up period, typically a few days, during which a borrower can exit by repaying only principal and proportionate interest, without penalty.
source: RBI Guidelines on Digital Lending, 2022
required_correction: None, though could be more precise: RBI mandates a minimum 3-day cooling-off period for loans with tenor of 7 days or more, and a minimum 1-day period for loans with tenor under 7 days, during which the borrower can exit by paying only principal plus proportionate APR.

article_title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
claim: Report harassment to the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) or call 1930, and separately file a complaint with the RBI if the lender claims to be a registered NBFC, since RBI has a formal grievance process for regulated entities.
source: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (1930 helpline) and RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme
required_correction: None — 1930/cybercrime.gov.in are correct, and RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme is the correct formal channel, but note it requires exhausting the lender's own internal Grievance Redressal Officer first (30-day window) before escalating to the RBI Ombudsman — the article could make this sequencing clearer.

article_title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
claim: A fraudulent loan taken through one of these apps can still get reported to credit bureaus in some cases if the lender has even informal bureau reporting arrangements, and unresolved default status can damage your credit score.
required_correction: Could not find an authoritative source confirming unregistered/fraudulent (non-RBI-regulated) loan apps have working credit bureau reporting arrangements — bureaus like CIBIL/Experian/CRIF/Equifax generally only accept data feeds from RBI-regulated 'Credit Institution' members, which unregistered fraudulent apps by definition are not. The claim risks misleading readers into overestimating a fake app's ability to formally damage their credit file; soften to note this is uncommon/disputed rather than presenting it as a confirmed 'can still happen' risk, or remove unless a specific documented case is cited.

article_title: How to Recognize a Fake Loan App Before It Drains Your Bank Account
claim: A regulated lender's onboarding uses Aadhaar-based e-KYC through UIDAI's own system rather than a generic upload field.
source: UIDAI e-KYC framework used by RBI-regulated lenders
required_correction: None — Aadhaar-based e-KYC via UIDAI's authentication system is the standard onboarding flow for RBI-regulated digital lenders and NBFCs.

article_title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
claim: A power bank typically delivers somewhere around 60 to 75 percent of its rated mAh as actual usable charge through the USB port.
source: Power bank efficiency analyses (Anker/eufy support documentation; independent power bank testing writeups)
required_correction: Most sources cite typical realistic usable output closer to 60-70% of rated capacity after 3.7V-to-5V boost conversion and PMIC losses (some low-quality units as low as 65% or worse); the article's upper bound of 75% is achievable with a high-efficiency boost converter (~85-92% efficient) but is on the optimistic edge rather than the typical case. Consider tightening the stated range to roughly 60-70% as the norm, noting 75%+ is possible only with premium components.

article_title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
claim: A BIS certification mark has been mandatory for power banks sold in India for several years now, since regulations tightened.
source: BIS Compulsory Registration Scheme for power banks, IS 13252 (Part 1):2010
required_correction: None — BIS registration for power banks became mandatory effective May 13, 2015 under the Compulsory Registration Scheme, confirming the article's 'mandatory for several years' framing (over a decade as of 2026); note a transition to the newer IS/IEC 62368-1:2023 standard runs until November 1, 2028.

article_title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
claim: DGCA/BCAS rules allow power banks only in cabin baggage, never checked baggage, and cap them at 100 watt-hours (roughly 27000mAh at nominal voltage) without special airline permission.
source: DGCA Civil Aviation Requirements on carriage of lithium batteries/power banks
required_correction: None — power banks/spare lithium batteries must be in cabin baggage only; up to 100Wh is allowed without airline approval, 100-160Wh requires prior airline approval, and above 160Wh is prohibited entirely, matching the article's figures. The mAh-to-Wh math (100Wh ÷ 3.7V × 1000 ≈ 27,027mAh) checks out correctly.

article_title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
claim: The cells inside a power bank run at roughly 3.7 volts, and you can estimate Wh by multiplying mAh by 3.7 and dividing by 1000.
source: Standard lithium-ion cell nominal voltage specification (Wh = mAh × V ÷ 1000)
required_correction: None — 3.7V is the standard nominal voltage for lithium-ion/lithium-polymer cells used in power banks, and the Wh = (mAh × V) ÷ 1000 formula is the correct standard conversion used by airlines and manufacturers.

article_title: Power Bank Buying Guide: What the mAh Number Does Not Tell You
claim: A power bank with two or three output ports does not give each port its full rated wattage simultaneously; total output is shared across ports.
source: General power bank/USB power-delivery specification behavior (shared internal power budget across multi-port designs)
required_correction: This is standard, widely-understood electrical behavior for multi-port power banks (shared internal power budget) but no single authoritative primary source was found beyond general manufacturer spec-sheet documentation; treat as an industry-standard technical fact rather than one needing a specific citation.

article_title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
claim: Browser extensions and price-tracking tools that log a product's price over weeks or months exist, and several of them work on Amazon India and Flipkart listings.
source: BuyHatke Price History / PriceHistory.app / other India-focused price trackers
required_correction: None — multiple functioning tools (BuyHatke, Price History, ProductHistory, PriceBefore) specifically track Amazon India and Flipkart price history and offer alerts, confirming the claim.

article_title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
claim: Countdown timers that reset after refreshing, or 'only 2 left' labels that persist across days, are a common tactic and should not influence a purchase decision.
source: India's Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 (CCPA, Consumer Protection Act 2019)
required_correction: None, but the article misses an opportunity to cite this directly: India's CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns (2023) explicitly name 'false urgency' — including countdown timers that reset on refresh — as one of 13 prohibited dark patterns, and the CCPA has since penalized platforms like Zepto, BookMyShow, IndiGo, and others for this. Naming this regulation would materially strengthen the article's credibility.

article_title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
claim: MRP is frequently set high on purpose and rarely reflects what the product sells for even outside sale periods.
required_correction: General market observation about pricing behavior, not a specific checkable statistic; no correction needed, though a cited example (e.g., a specific product category study) would strengthen it.

article_title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
claim: Some sellers briefly list a product at an inflated price for a short window right before a sale starts, purely so the sale price can be measured against that inflated number — a practice sometimes called price anchoring.
source: Price anchoring / reference-price manipulation practice, discussed in consumer-protection and dark-pattern literature
required_correction: The mechanism described (a brief price spike right before a sale to inflate the 'before' price) is a recognized manipulative pricing tactic discussed under India's dark-pattern and consumer-protection guidance, though it is more commonly termed 'reference pricing' or 'fake discounting' than 'price anchoring' in Indian regulatory literature specifically. No factual correction needed to the mechanism itself; minor terminology note only.

article_title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
claim: A ₹500 'free' bundled accessory that would sell standalone for ₹150 is not really ₹500 of savings, no matter what the bundle page claims.
required_correction: Illustrative hypothetical example used to make a valid general point about bundle-value inflation; not a specific checkable claim, no correction needed.

article_title: How to Tell If a Deal Price Online Is Actually a Discount
claim: An unusually steep discount from a third-party marketplace seller with few reviews or a recently created storefront carries more risk than the same discount from the platform's own official store.
required_correction: Reasonable general risk-assessment advice, not a specific statistic; no correction needed.

article_title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
claim: A traditional HDD caps sequential speeds around 100 to 160 MB/s, while a SATA SSD pushes sequential speeds around 500 MB/s.
source: Benchmark discussions of typical 5400/7200 RPM laptop HDD and SATA SSD sequential throughput (Tom's Hardware/PCPartPicker community benchmark data)
required_correction: None — typical laptop HDDs (5400/7200 RPM) deliver roughly 80-200 MB/s sequential depending on model/RPM, consistent with the article's '100 to 160 MB/s' range, while SATA SSDs commonly reach 500-600 MB/s, matching the article's '~500 MB/s' figure.

article_title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
claim: NVMe SSDs are faster than SATA SSDs on paper, sometimes by four to six times in raw sequential speed.
source: NVMe vs SATA SSD benchmark comparisons (IBM, GigeNET, TechCompare)
required_correction: A '4-6x' gap is a reasonable description for typical/budget PCIe Gen3 NVMe drives (roughly 2,000-3,500 MB/s vs. ~550-600 MB/s SATA), but high-end Gen4/Gen5 NVMe drives reach 7,000-14,000+ MB/s, a 12-25x gap — larger than the article states. Since this article targets budget laptops, the 4-6x figure is defensible for the relevant drive class, but the phrase 'on paper' slightly understates how large the gap can get on premium NVMe hardware; consider clarifying this is specifically about entry-level NVMe drives.

article_title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
claim: eMMC is technically flash storage but noticeably slower than a real SSD, closer to a fast HDD than to SATA SSD speeds.
source: eMMC vs SSD vs HDD speed comparisons (Windows Central, CDW, Spacehop)
required_correction: eMMC typically delivers roughly 200-400 MB/s sequential, which is meaningfully faster than most laptop HDDs (80-200 MB/s) but far below SATA SSD (500-600 MB/s). The article's framing ('closer to a fast HDD than to SATA SSD speed') somewhat understates eMMC's real advantage over HDD in raw sequential throughput — the more accurate summary is that eMMC sits clearly between HDD and SATA SSD, but its poor random I/O and lack of a real controller make it feel much closer to HDD in everyday responsiveness, which the article correctly emphasizes elsewhere.

article_title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
claim: SSDs slow down as they fill up; keeping at least 10-15% of an SSD free helps it maintain its performance advantage over time.
source: SSD TRIM/overprovisioning performance guidance (Seagate, Phison, The SSD Review)
required_correction: None — sources broadly converge on keeping roughly 10-20% of an SSD free (many recommend staying under ~80-85% full) to preserve TRIM/garbage-collection headroom and avoid write-amplification slowdowns; the article's 10-15% figure sits comfortably within this consensus range.

article_title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
claim: A laptop with an HDD boots in over a minute versus under 20 seconds for one with an SSD.
required_correction: Presented as a general illustrative figure without a citation or specific test methodology (OS, hardware generation, background startup apps all affect boot time significantly). Directionally correct that SSDs boot dramatically faster, but the specific numbers ('under 20 seconds' vs 'over a minute') should either be sourced to a specific benchmark/model comparison or softened to avoid implying a precise, universal figure.

article_title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
claim: Swapping in a SATA SSD is often a bigger felt improvement than a RAM upgrade on the same machine.
required_correction: Comparative subjective judgment about perceived performance improvement, not independently checkable as stated; no correction needed, though it aligns with common enthusiast/repair-shop consensus for storage-bottlenecked systems.

article_title: SSD vs HDD for a Budget Laptop: Where the Money Should Actually Go
claim: On a tight budget, prioritizing SSD over RAM over CPU generation, in that order, tends to produce the most noticeable everyday improvement per rupee spent.
required_correction: A prioritization recommendation/value judgment, not a specific checkable fact; no correction needed.
